Article Title: iPhone Fold, Pro and Pro Max: Apple’s biggest 'iPhone gamble' in years gets a launch date
Article Text:
Apple could do for foldables what it has done before

Where will the regular iPhone go

Apple has sent invites for its 'September event'. iPhone-makers 'Surprise and shine' event is set for September 9. Apple September iPhone event is usually the most predictable date on the technology calendar. New iPhones arrive, the Pro models get the biggest upgrades, cameras improve and prices are debated. This year could be very different.If reports around Apple's 2026 plans are accurate, the company could use its September event for arguably the biggest restructuring of the iPhone portfolio in years. Two changes stand out: Apple is expected to finally enter the foldable smartphone market, while the regular iPhone 18 may not launch alongside the Pro models at all.That would leave the September lineup dominated by Apple's most expensive phones — the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and its first foldable iPhone. The standard iPhone 18 is instead expected to arrive in spring 2027.And all of this is happening just as the smartphone industry enters an uncomfortable new era of higher hardware prices.Apple will be arriving extremely late to foldables. Samsung has been selling them since 2019, while Google, Oppo, Honor and others have spent years solving problems around hinges, durability, thickness and screen creases.Yet foldables remain a niche category, accounting for less than 3% of global smartphone sales. That is precisely why Apple's arrival matters.The company has repeatedly entered categories after rivals and then helped push them towards the mainstream. The Apple Watch was hardly the first smartwatch, nor were AirPods the first wireless earbuds. Apple's strength lies in taking an existing idea, making it easier to understand and putting it in front of a huge installed base. IDC has forecast global foldable smartphone shipments to grow about 30% in 2026, driven significantly by Apple's entry. Counterpoint has separately projected a 20% increase.For Samsung, this creates both an opportunity and a problem. Samsung executives have publicly welcomed Apple's expected entry, arguing that another global player will expand the category. There is logic to that: Apple could effectively validate a form factor Samsung has spent seven years on and has also largely succeeded.But Samsung also risks losing something important — ownership of the foldable conversation. Until now, a premium book-style foldable has largely meant Galaxy Z Fold. Apple entering the category changes that. Also, Apple is unlikely to compete on price. Current expectations put the first foldable iPhone above $2,000, with some estimates stretching towards $2,500. That could make it one of the most expensive mainstream smartphones Apple has ever sold. Oddly, that price may help rather than hurt its strategic purpose. Apple does not need the Fold to become the biggest-selling iPhone immediately. It needs the device to create excitement at the top of the portfolio and establish a new premium tier above the Pro Max.The second change may be less glamorous but equally important. Apple is reportedly splitting its iPhone launch cycle. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are expected in September, alongside the foldable, while the regular iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e could move to spring 2027.For consumers, that means something unusual: there may be no new "vanilla" iPhone at Apple's biggest hardware event of the year. For Apple, however, the strategy makes considerable sense.The September event would become an unapologetically premium showcase. Instead of a $799-ish entry point sitting beside far more expensive devices, attention would remain on models carrying the highest margins and biggest technological upgrades.It could also smooth Apple's sales cycle. Rather than concentrating nearly the entire iPhone launch in one quarter, Apple can create another major upgrade window six months later. But there may be another reason why separating cheaper and expensive iPhones suddenly makes sense: RAMageddon.AI-driven demand for memory is pushing DRAM and NAND prices sharply higher. IDC says memory can account for 15-20% of the bill of materials of a mid-range smartphone and 10-15% of a flagship. It expects manufacturers to respond by increasing prices, cutting specifications or doing both.Apple itself is reportedly examining cost reductions for the regular iPhone 18, including cheaper display specifications and changes to chips and components, as RAM costs rise. It is part of a much broader smartphone trend. Oppo, Vivo, Realme, OnePlus, Samsung and others have already begun raising prices in India as memory and component costs increase. Qualcomm, too, is raising processor prices from September.Premium phones are better placed to absorb those increases because component costs represent a smaller proportion of their selling price. Which makes Apple's expected September strategy particularly interesting. At precisely the moment when smartphones are becoming more expensive, Apple may be removing its mainstream model from its biggest launch and doubling down on the expensive end. September 2026 could therefore be remembered not simply as the year Apple finally made a folding phone. It could be the moment the iPhone itself became a more deliberately premium product.
Article Summary: Apple is expected to finally enter the foldable smartphone market. The regular iPhone 18 may not launch alongside the Pro models at all. That would leave the September lineup dominated by the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max and its first foldable iPhone. The standard iPhone 18 is instead expected to arrive in spring 2027.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos: “If you decide that you’re going to do only the things you know...” - the lesson behind taking risks
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos

“If you decide that you’re going to do only the things you know are going to work, you’re going to leave a lot of opportunity on the table.”

What does the quote mean

How Bezos turned an uncertain internet idea into Amazon

The difference between a calculated test and a gamble

The importance of reversible decisions

How small experiments can turn uncertainty into clarity

A practical way to judge an uncertain idea

Lessons to learn from Jeff Bezos's quote

Not knowing whether something will work does not mean it will fail.

Trying unproven ideas can create opportunities that would otherwise be missed.

Failure can provide valuable information for future decisions.

Some successful ideas begin as uncertain experiments.

Focusing only on proven paths can limit creativity and discovery.

Taking risks does not mean acting recklessly; it means accepting uncertainty while exploring possibilities.

Unexpected opportunities often appear when people are willing to test ideas without guaranteed results.

There is a certain comfort in knowing how something will turn out. When a decision has worked for someone else, the risks seem easier to judge and the next step feels less uncertain. At work, in business or even in everyday life, people often prefer choices that come with some evidence behind them. Trying something unfamiliar is different. There may be no guarantee that the effort will pay off, and sometimes the safest-looking option feels like the sensible one. Yet choosing only what is already proven can also mean passing up possibilities that have not had a chance to reveal themselves.Many opportunities begin as ideas that are difficult to assess from the start. They may succeed, fail or lead somewhere unexpected. That tension between certainty and possibility sits at the centre of a widely quoted observation from Amazon founder Jeff Bezos about knowing what will work and what might be worth trying.Bezos made the remark during a 2008 WIRED interview while discussing Amazon's approach to experimentation and the company's A9 search project.The context matters because he was not describing success as something that comes from making a series of perfectly safe decisions. He was explaining why a company may need to pursue ideas without knowing beforehand whether they will succeed.At its simplest, Bezos is pointing to the cost of excessive certainty. If a person agrees to do something only after knowing that it will work, the number of available choices becomes quite small. Established methods are easier to justify because their results are already visible. New ideas do not have that advantage.A new product, service or business may look uncertain precisely because nobody has tested it properly. Waiting until the outcome becomes obvious can therefore create a strange problem: by the time an opportunity is proven, much of the uncertainty has already disappeared and others may have noticed it too.Bezos's point is not that uncertainty automatically makes an idea worthwhile. It is that uncertainty alone is not a sufficient reason to reject it.When Bezos founded Amazon in 1994, internet retail was still a relatively unfamiliar concept. He had been working at D.E. Shaw in New York when he became interested in the rapid expansion of the internet. He eventually left the firm and moved to Seattle, where he began building an online business.Amazon initially concentrated on books. The choice was practical in some ways: there were millions of titles, while physical bookshops could only carry a fraction of them. But the larger proposition convincing people to buy books through a website was still unproven.Amazon opened its online bookstore in 1995. The company would later expand into many other areas, but the early decision illustrates the kind of uncertainty Bezos was talking about. There was no guarantee that online shopping would become an ordinary part of consumer life.The quotation can easily be read as an argument for taking bigger risks. That would miss an important part of the idea. Trying something uncertain does not require committing everything to it.A business might develop a small version of a product, introduce it to a limited audience and examine what happens. If customers respond positively, the company has a reason to invest further. If they do not, the cost of the experiment can be kept within reasonable limits.This way of working creates a middle ground between doing nothing and making a huge bet. The uncertainty remains, but it becomes something that can be investigated.Another idea associated with Bezos's management philosophy is the distinction between reversible and difficult-to-reverse decisions. Some choices are relatively easy to change. If a small experiment does not work, the company can stop it. A different approach can then be tried.Other decisions carry much larger consequences. Those may require extensive information, consultation and preparation before anything is changed.Bezos has argued that organisations can sometimes slow themselves down by treating every decision as though it were permanent. When a choice can be reversed without major damage, there can be a case for moving sooner and learning from the result.That provides a useful qualification to his quote. The aim is not to remove caution. It is to avoid demanding the same level of certainty from every decision.The same tension appears in ordinary decisions. Someone considering a career change may want evidence that the new field will definitely suit them before taking the first step. A person thinking about starting a small business may wait for proof that customers will buy. Someone learning a new skill may hesitate because there is no guarantee it will lead anywhere.In each case, certainty may not arrive before action. A smaller trial can sometimes provide the missing information. A short course can test an interest. A small business project can reveal whether customers exist. A trial period in a new role can provide a clearer picture than speculation from the outside.The point is not to act without thinking. It is to recognise that some information can only be obtained by doing.The quote can be understood as a warning against making certainty the entry requirement for every new idea.Before rejecting an unfamiliar option, it can be useful to ask a few basic questions. What would be learned by trying it? Can the idea be tested on a small scale? How expensive would failure be? Can the decision be reversed? What evidence would justify continuing?Those questions turn an abstract idea about risk into something more practical.They also separate experimentation from impulsiveness. There is a difference between saying yes to everything and being willing to investigate something that has not yet proved itself.
Article Summary: Jeff Bezos made the remark while discussing Amazon's approach to experimentation and the company's A9 search project. He was explaining why a company may need to pursue ideas without knowing beforehand whether they will succeed. The quote can easily be read as an argument for taking bigger risks. Trying something uncertain does not require committing everything to it.

Article Title: 6 ChatGPT image prompts to turn your sibling bond into a movie poster or postcard this Raksha Bandhan
Article Text:
Happy Raksha Bandhan

Here are six prompt ideas worth trying this year

Some memories only make sense to one other person. The story behind an old photograph. A joke that stopped landing with everyone else years ago. A dance routine you still nail without missing a beat. The one snack you will still never share. Distance and time may separate siblings, but these small, specific memories have a way of pulling them right back together.This Raksha Bandhan, ChatGPT Images 2.0 offers a new way to give those memories shape. A years-old inside joke can become a comic strip. A shared childhood fantasy can drop both siblings into a movie or superhero universe. A sibling relationship can even be imagined decades into the future — or a familiar memory can be turned into a Rakhi postcard for a sibling who's far away this year.Because sometimes, the most meaningful gift isn't the most expensive one. It's the one only the two of you would ever fully understand.1. Give your sibling the award they actually deserveSkip the generic "Best Brother" or "Best Sister" titles. Every family has its own, far more specific honors worth handing out — think Champion Food Stealer, Family Secret Keeper, Emergency Advice-Giver, or Person Most Likely to Call Only WhenThey Need Something.The idea: upload a photo of your sibling and ask ChatGPT to design a premium-looking award poster built around one of these invented titles, styled to feel affectionate and celebratory, with festive touches like a rakhi, mithai, or marigolds worked into the design.2. Turn your sibling story into a movie posterEvery sibling relationship already has enough drama, comedy, and plot twists to fill a film. This prompt turns that dynamic into a poster.The idea: use a shared photo to reimagine you and your sibling as the leads of an Indian movie poster, with a title of your choosing. The goal is to preserve your actual faces while capturing the mix of rivalry and closeness that defines the relationship, styled with cinematic lighting and festive colour.3. Become the superhero duo you always claimed to beOne sibling always finds the lost charger. The other always handles the parents. Together, that's basically a superhero team already.The idea: reimagine yourselves as a sibling superhero duo, with costumes designed around each person's personality, set in a vivid, cinematic scene — with a rakhi worked subtly into the costume or visual design itself.4. Turn your most repeated argument into a comic stripSome sibling disagreements deserve to be preserved for the historical record — whoever controls the remote, borrows clothes without asking, claims the front seat, or takes the last piece of food.The idea: turn that recurring argument into a four-panel comic strip using your own photos as reference, showing the fight, a moment of secretly helping each other anyway, sharing a favorite food, and ending on a Raksha Bandhan truce.5. Celebrate Raksha Bandhan together, even from different citiesNot every sibling pair will be in the same room this year. For siblings living in different cities or countries, this prompt merges both celebrations into one image.The idea: generate a single split-scene postcard connecting both locations, with natural, recognizable faces, visual details tied to each city, and a symbolic rakhi thread running between the two halves of the image.6. See what Raksha Bandhan might look like 40 years from nowThe arguments may evolve. The teasing almost certainly won't. This prompt imagines the same sibling pair, the same rakhi ritual, decades down the line.The idea: age both siblings naturally while preserving their features and dynamic, placed in a warm setting that blends future and tradition — a rakhi, a thali, mithai, and old family photographs all in the frame.
Article Summary: Raksha Bandhan, ChatGPT Images 2.0 offers a new way to give memories shape. A years-old inside joke can become a comic strip. A shared childhood fantasy can drop both siblings into a movie universe. A sibling relationship can even be imagined decades into the future.

Article Title: Hyundai may sell Boston Dynamics robots through local auto dealers: What CEO has to say
Article Text:
Factory deployments and next-generation Atlas robot

Hyundai races to deploy humanoid hardware

Hyundai dealerships in your neighborhood may eventually showcase and sell humanoid and quadruped robots alongside cars. Speaking during the automaker’s investor day, Hyundai CEO José Muñoz revealed that the company is exploring plans to leverage its franchised dealer network to retail advanced robots built by Boston Dynamics, as per a report by a report by Business Insider. Muñoz added that the automaker’s financial arm, Hyundai Capital, is assessing whether to offer consumer financing programs for robotics in the same way it finances vehicle purchases.The roadmap builds on Hyundai Motor Group’s 2021 acquisition of an 80% controlling stake in Boston Dynamics, a transaction that valued the robotics pioneer at $1.1 billion.Boston Dynamics already markets commercial systems such as Spot, a four-legged robotic platform used for industrial surveying and maintenance, and Stretch, a wheeled, single-armed unit built to unload cargo from shipping containers and freight trucks. Notably, Hyundai utilises Spot across its manufacturing facilities for predictive inspections, including checking vehicle exteriors within the paint and weld shops at its Georgia Metaplant, where the company manufactures the Ioniq 5 and Ioniq 9 electric vehicles.The next major milestone centres on Atlas, Boston Dynamics’ flagship humanoid robot equipped with a 180-degree swiveling torso. Muñoz confirmed that Hyundai is preparing to begin mass production of the humanoid model.Hyundai’s push into robotics mirrors a wider movement across the automotive sector to integrate autonomous humanoids into factory floors. Companies like BMW and Figure have developed humanoid machines to handle and sort heavy automotive components in Spartanburg, South Carolina.Similarly, Toyota and Agility Robotics have finalised a deployment agreement to integrate its bipedal robots into the carmakers’ vehicle manufacturing facilities in Canada. Mercedes-Benz has begun testing Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid across its plants to deliver component bins and conduct parts inspections.Tesla is building out dedicated assembly lines for its Optimus humanoid inside its Fremont, California plant.
Article Summary: Hyundai is exploring plans to leverage its franchised dealer network to retail advanced robots built by Boston Dynamics. The automaker’s financial arm, Hyundai Capital, is assessing whether to offer consumer financing programs for robotics in the same way it finances vehicle purchases. The next major milestone centres on Atlas, Boston Dynamics’ flagship humanoid robot.

Article Title: Apple pitches Mac mini, Studio for the age of local AI
Article Text:
Apple Mac mini

New Delhi: Apple is making a stronger pitch for the Mac as a local AI computing machine, positioning its new Mac mini and Mac Studio as systems capable of running AI models, automated workflows and agentic workloads without relying entirely on the cloud.TOI spoke to Apple and learned that “desk-side” AI compute is emerging as a key use case, as developers and enterprises increasingly look to run language models and AI workflows locally instead of sending every task to large cloud-based systems.The shift is important because the AI boom has so far been dominated by hyperscale data centres packed with expensive GPUs. But as models become more efficient and desktop hardware gets more capable, a growing number of AI workloads can be handled locally, particularly for development, testing and inference.Apple is looking to tap into this transition through its unified memory architecture and tightly integrated hardware and software stack. The company is pitching Macs as machines that can keep more AI workloads on-device, potentially reducing dependence on cloud infrastructure while also offering advantages around latency and data privacy.The new Mac mini comes with either Apple’s M6 or M5 Pro chip. Apple says the M6 version delivers up to four times faster AI performance and twice the graphics and storage performance compared with the previous generation.It starts with 16GB unified memory, configurable up to 32GB, while the M5 Pro version supports up to 64GB. The machines also get Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 and faster Ethernet, while Thunderbolt 5 on the M5 Pro model allows multiple Mac minis to be clustered together to run larger AI models locally.The Mac mini with M6 starts at Rs 99,900 in India, while the M5 Pro version starts at Rs 2,09,900. Both will go on sale from September 22.At the higher end, the new Mac Studio comes with M5 Max and M5 Ultra chips and is aimed at developers, AI researchers, data scientists and creative professionals. Apple claims up to 4.3 times faster AI performance, along with faster graphics and storage. The M5 Ultra version can be configured with up to 512GB of unified memory, allowing significantly larger AI models to be loaded and run locally.Mac Studio with M5 Max starts at Rs 2,79,900, while the M5 Ultra model starts at Rs 6,29,900. The 512GB configuration will be available later in October.Apple’s broader bet is that the Mac can carve out a role in an AI computing stack that increasingly combines cloud, edge and local processing — not replacing massive GPU servers, but serving as a powerful desk-side system for building, testing and running increasingly capable AI workloads.
Article Summary: Apple is positioning its new Mac mini and Mac Studio as systems capable of running AI models, automated workflows and agentic workloads without relying entirely on the cloud. Article Title: Dropbox co-CEO Ashraf Alkarmi’s simple rule for staying focused: I do not go to meetings that are not related to…
Article Text:
Image credit: LinkedIn

How Alkarmi narrowed his focus after joining Dropbox

Dropbox co-CEO Ashraf Alkarmi has developed a time-management system that starts with identifying five priorities each quarter. The approach also shapes what he chooses to skip. "Sometimes I get meetings that are not related to these things, and I don't go," Alkarmi said, describing how the list determines not just where he spends his time, but where he doesn't.In a statement to Business Insider, Alkarmi said the five priorities function as a filter for his schedule. "I pick things that I can make significant progress on in that quarter," he said. "And so it becomes a filter for how I prioritise my time." He shares the list with his team, administration, and chief of staff so that others understand where his attention is directed. According to Alkarmi, those priorities take precedence over competing demands that arise during the quarter.Alkarmi joined Dropbox in 2024 after holding leadership roles at Vimeo and Meta. He became co-CEO in May, alongside Dropbox founder Drew Houston, and is expected to become the company's sole CEO eventually.When he joined Dropbox, Alkarmi said he encountered a wide range of tasks spanning multiple business categories. To manage the scope of the role, he narrowed his focus to five key areas, including people, the business, and performance.On the business side, Alkarmi said he reviewed available data and identified reducing customer churn as a priority to make what he described as "meaningful progress" within the first quarter. He said he tracks his top five priorities using the work management tool Trello.Beyond guiding how he allocates his time, Alkarmi said the list also helps him decide what does not warrant his attention. He does not add meetings unrelated to his current priorities to his schedule, and he said he will send a delegate in his place when appropriate.
Article Summary: Dropbox co-CEO Ashraf Alkarmi has developed a time-management system that starts with identifying five priorities each quarter. He shares the list with his team, administration, and chief of staff so that others understand where his attention is directed. The approach also shapes what he chooses to skip.
